headline: Massachusetts approves tougher nursing-home ownership reviews
dek: New rules will give public health officials more tools to examine operators’ finances, management companies, care records and out-of-state histories before approving licenses or transfers.
body: Massachusetts public health officials approved a new set of nursing-home regulations Wednesday that will expand the state’s review of who owns, manages and operates long-term-care facilities. The changes are designed to move the licensure process beyond the condition of an individual building and toward a fuller review of the people and companies behind it, including their finances, litigation and care records in other states. The [Massachusetts Department of Public Health’s Oct. 14 meeting notice](https://www.mass.gov/event/public-health-council-meeting-october-14-2026-10-14-2026) lists the amendments to the state’s long-term-care licensure and facility standards regulations as final regulations approved by the Public Health Council.

The rules are not effective immediately. They now go to Secretary of State William Galvin’s office for promulgation, a step that Public Health Commissioner Robbie Goldstein said is expected in early November, according to [WBUR and the State House News Service](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/15/nursing-home-new-licenses-care-regulations). After that process, applicants for new licenses and people seeking to transfer licenses will face enhanced suitability reviews. The department also expects to examine management companies that contract to run facilities and licensees seeking renewal.

The practical change is that ownership and management structures will become part of the state’s safety review. The regulations define a management company as an entity hired to manage a long-term-care facility for compensation and require facilities to report changes in financial status. The department has also begun surveying owners to identify where management companies are used, WBUR reported. That information matters because a facility’s finances can involve landlords, related service companies, investors and other entities whose decisions affect staffing, maintenance and resident care.

The framework implements a 2024 Massachusetts law that directs the Department of Public Health to consider an applicant’s criminal and civil litigation history, financial capacity and record of providing quality care. The [law’s text](https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartI/TitleXVI/Chapter111/Section71) says the review may include owners and management companies, recorded liens or unpaid fees and taxes, federal quality measures, and the operator’s history in Massachusetts and other states. It also requires the department to consider private-equity involvement when assessing the quality record of an applicant or potential transferee.

The new suitability criteria are intended to give regulators a clearer basis for saying an operator is not responsible or suitable. According to the State House News Service account, disqualifying circumstances can include jeopardizing residents’ health or safety, lacking sufficient financial resources to provide services, maintaining substandard care, or having a 50% or greater interest or corporate tie to a facility whose license was suspended, denied or revoked. Other factors that can weigh heavily include failing to report abuse or neglect, a conviction or guilty plea, obtaining a license through fraud or misrepresentation, or litigation tied to long-term-care operations.

The timing follows a high-profile dispute over whether Massachusetts previously had enough information about nursing-home owners. The administration’s regulatory push accelerated after reporting examined the state’s approvals of RegalCare acquisitions and the quality problems at some of its facilities. On Oct. 13, the Department of Public Health announced its intent to revoke the licenses associated with all 12 RegalCare homes, saying owner Eliyahu “Eli” Mirlis was not suitable or responsible to operate long-term-care facilities. That separate administrative case remains a proceeding; the new regulations do not by themselves decide its outcome.

The rules also cover more than ownership. The Public Health Council agenda describes amendments involving long-term-care standards, certified medication aides, outbreak-response plans and small-house nursing homes. Those provisions could affect how facilities organize care and how regulators evaluate compliance, although the exact effect will depend on the final text and the department’s implementation procedures after promulgation. The state’s 2024 law also set two-year license terms and called for at least one periodic, resident-centered inspection each year.

For residents and families, the immediate result is not a new facility rating or an automatic change in care. It is a stronger screening process for future applicants, ownership transfers and troubled facilities. Goldstein told the Public Health Council that regulators are developing ways to engage more actively with facilities that have significant complaints or quality concerns, including possible temporary management, consultants and corrective-action plans. The next concrete milestone is publication of the regulations by the Secretary of State; after that, the department will have to show how it applies the new financial, ownership and care-history standards in individual cases.
